summary:
Metal encapsulation of niobium thin films with gold or palladium/gold significantly alters bulk superconducting properties beyond surface passivation, including residual resistivity ratio, transition temperature, upper critical field, and London penetration depth. Comprehensive measurements of 110–163 nm thick Nb films on sapphire via resistivity, magnetization, magneto-optical imaging, and TDR reveal that Au-capped films exhibit the highest residual resistivity ratio ($	ext{RRR} \
approx 34$ for epitaxial, $\
approx 24$ for sputtered) and transition temperature while showing the lowest upper critical field, London penetration depth, and critical current density.
motivation: Understanding the mechanisms behind metal encapsulation's effectiveness in improving transmon qubit coherence (previously reported as $\\sim 5\\times$ improvement with Ta capping) requires investigation of how capping affects bulk Nb properties, since disorder throughout the film contributes significantly to decoherence alongside surface oxides.
method: Six Nb films (bare, Au-capped, and PdAu-capped sputtered samples at 150–163 nm; bare and Au-capped epitaxial samples at 110–120 nm) were characterized via four-probe resistivity, vibrating sample magnetometry with field parallel to the film, magneto-optical Faraday imaging of flux penetration, tunnel diode resonator measurements of London and Campbell penetration depths, and transport measurements of $H_{c2}(T)$ with TOF-SIMS compositional profiling.
result: Au-capped films achieve $T_c$ values closest to the clean limit, suppress themagnetic avalanches entirely, and exhibit the lowest critical current density ($j_c$) and Campbell penetration depth ($\\lambda_C$) at $H = 0.4$ T, while bare Nb films show the highest disorder ($	ext{RRR} \\approx 5$), highest $H_{c2}(0)$, and strong thermomagnetic instabilities; oxygen concentration is $\\sim 10\\times$ higher in bare Nb than Au-capped sputtered films, correlating with disorder-driven $T_c$ suppression described by the anisotropic multiband BCS theory for Nb.
